Historians of Greek philosophy generally believe that Leucippus was a contemporary of Empedocles and Anaxagoras in the fifth century BCE. Democritus was born in Abdera, in Thrace in northern Greece, late in the fifth century BCE. He lived to a great age, and some accounts say he lived for more than a hundred years. He travelled to Egypt, Babylon, and Persia, and even reached India, gaining much from these journeys through the East. His works have not survived in their original form. What remains are relatively short fragments, most of them preserved in quotations by Aristotle. These quotations and the historical evidence suggest that his largest work was The Great World-System, in which he set out his view of the structure of the universe.↩︎

Science in later centuries confirmed this hypothesis of Democritus. Torricelli’s experiment in 1643 demonstrated that a vacuum really exists, finally overturning the Aristotelian mechanics that held that nature abhors a vacuum. Modern science has also established the principle that nothing comes from nothing, that no existing thing can simply vanish into nothing, and that changes in matter occur through the joining or separation of particles. This was already part of Democritus’s conception when he developed his atomic theory. It also contains the basis of the modern physical principles of the conservation of matter and energy.↩︎
